paragraphs: Personalized intervention policies use predictions about who would benefit from treatment to decide whom to help. Auditing their fairness creates a special difficulty: an individual's outcome under the treatment they did not receive is unobserved. Consequently, even experimental data cannot directly reveal the individual benefit labels needed to calculate standard fairness measures such as true positive rates.

The paper establishes this identification problem and then studies what additional assumptions make an audit possible. Under monotone treatment response, an assumption that rules out treatment changing outcomes in the adverse direction, the authors show that the fairness quantities can be uniquely identified. That conclusion depends on the assumption; it does not remove the underlying absence of individual counterfactual outcomes.

The authors also derive sharp bounds when monotonicity is allowed to fail to varying degrees. These bounds support a sensitivity analysis rather than requiring unquestioned acceptance of monotonicity. Partially identified ROC and xROC curves turn the results into auditing tools, illustrated with French job training data.
neurips-2019-assessing-disparate-impact-.tldr: The paper shows why auditing personalized interventions requires causal assumptions and provides exact identification under monotonicity plus bounds when it fails.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions where actions have adversarially chosen losses, observations are incomplete, and changing actions carries a fixed cost. A feedback graph describes which observations become available after an action. The learner therefore has to balance gathering useful information, choosing low-loss actions, and avoiding expensive switching.

The authors introduce two algorithms for the informed setting. Their strongest pseudo-regret bound scales as the cube root of the graph's domination number times the number of rounds to the two-thirds power, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The domination number captures how small a collection of actions can provide coverage of the feedback graph. Using this quantity substantially improves the previous bound, which depended on the graph's independence number.

Matching lower bounds establish corresponding limits on achievable performance for the result studied. The paper also considers access to partial counterfactual feedback and gives an algorithm with improved policy regret bounds in that setting. Together, the results connect the structure of available information to learning performance when switching itself is costly.
neurips-2019-bandits-with-feedback-graph.tldr: New bandit algorithms use feedback-graph structure to improve regret guarantees when changing actions incurs a cost.

paragraphs: Object detection depends on proposing image regions that are likely to contain objects. Conventional region proposal networks use multiple predefined anchors with different sizes and shapes. This paper addresses both the heuristic choice of those anchors and the problem of keeping image features aligned with the regions they describe.

Cascade RPN starts with one anchor at each location and refines it through multiple stages. The stages progressively tighten the criteria for positive training samples, beginning with an anchor-free measure and then using anchor-based measures. An adaptive convolution receives both image features and anchors, allowing the anchors to guide which features are sampled as the regions change.

A two-stage implementation raises average recall by 13.4 points over the conventional RPN and is reported to surpass existing proposal methods. Incorporating it into Fast R-CNN and Faster R-CNN improves detection mean average precision by 3.1 and 3.5 points, respectively. These results show that the proposal improvements also benefit the subsequent detection task.
neurips-2019-cascade-rpn-delving-into-hi.tldr: Cascade RPN improves object proposals through staged anchor refinement and convolution that adapts its feature sampling to the anchors.

paragraphs: A model of a joint distribution describes variables together, but using that model to fill in only some variables poses a separate problem. The paper calls this co-generation: holding the given variables fixed while seeking the most likely configuration of the remaining ones. This can be computationally demanding even when the distribution itself can be modeled.

The authors investigate co-generation specifically for generative adversarial networks. They distinguish this setting from classical distribution models, where related inference problems have received considerably more attention. The central challenge is therefore how to use a GAN for constrained inference, beyond its role in generating complete samples from a learned distribution.

To address the challenges they identify, the authors develop a co-generation algorithm combining annealed importance sampling with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. They report substantial improvements over classical gradient-based methods on synthetic data and on CelebA and LSUN. The findings support this sampling-based approach for the evaluated co-generation problems, giving GANs a way to infer missing configurations conditioned on supplied information.
neurips-2019-co-generation-with-gans-usi.tldr: An algorithm combining annealed importance sampling and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo improves conditional configuration inference with GANs in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Unsupervised word translation aligns the word-vector spaces of two languages without starting from known translation pairs. The usual process has two parts: matching the distributions to create an initial dictionary, then using that dictionary to refine the alignment. Evaluating only the final alignment can obscure which part of the process actually produces an improvement.

This paper isolates the initial distribution-matching step. The authors compare methods on language pairs for which previous reports showed inconsistent training stability and evaluation results. In this comparison, ordinary GANs outperform newer distribution-matching techniques in both precision and robustness. The result challenges the interpretation that newer complete systems necessarily start from better initial matches.

The authors attribute the reported advances of the more recent methods to their refinement procedures. Combining ordinary GANs with those refinement techniques achieves state-of-the-art performance in their study. The practical contribution is a clearer account of where progress comes from: a strong existing initialization method can benefit from improvements made elsewhere in the pipeline.
neurips-2019-comparing-unsupervised-word.tldr: Separating initialization from refinement reveals that ordinary GANs provide stronger initial word alignments than newer methods in the studied comparisons.

paragraphs: Vector instructions let a processor apply one instruction to multiple data elements. Compilers exploit this capability by grouping compatible scalar operations into vector operations. In superword level parallelism vectorization, deciding which instructions to pack together matters, and the handcrafted strategies used by compilers can produce suboptimal choices.

An earlier approach formulated instruction packing as an integer linear program. This paper asks whether a graph neural network can learn to imitate the optimal decisions made by that formulation. The learned policy uses the optimization-based solution as its teacher, turning instruction packing into a decision problem that can be learned from expert choices.

The resulting vectorization schemes outperform industry compiler heuristics in both estimated cost and measured runtime in the reported tests. Against LLVM, the policy achieves a 22.6% higher average reduction in cost under LLVM's own cost model. On the NAS benchmark suite, its geometric mean runtime speedup over LLVM's SLP vectorizer is 1.015 times. These are distinct findings: improved estimated cost accompanies a smaller measured execution-time gain.
neurips-2019-compiler-auto-vectorization.tldr: A graph neural network imitates optimization-based instruction packing and improves vectorization cost estimates and runtime over LLVM's SLP heuristics.

paragraphs: Cross-modal learning connects information across different forms of data. The paper examines whether networks learning these connections can be fooled by tiny input changes, extending the concern about adversarial examples to cross-modal analysis. Its focus is retrieval using cross-modal hashing, where learned representations support finding related items across modalities.

The proposed method, CMLA, learns adversarial samples while incorporating two kinds of similarity constraints. One concerns relationships within a modality, and the other concerns relationships across modalities. Bringing both into adversarial sample learning ties the perturbations to the relationships that the target system is meant to capture.

Experiments on two cross-modal benchmark datasets show that CMLA's examples effectively fool a target deep cross-modal hashing network. The same examples also have a defensive use: incorporating them into adversarial training substantially improves the target network's robustness. The contribution therefore links a demonstrated vulnerability with a training method that strengthens the evaluated system against adversarial samples, rather than treating attack generation as an end in itself.
neurips-2019-cross-modal-learning-with-a.tldr: CMLA generates effective adversarial examples for cross-modal retrieval and uses them in training to improve the target network's robustness.

paragraphs: Neural spiking data can be represented as point processes, whose intensity functions describe how the rate of events changes. Modeling these functions requires flexibility while respecting constraints such as nonnegativity. The paper proposes Deep Random Splines as an alternative to Gaussian processes, which can be difficult to scale and adapt to certain shape constraints.

A Deep Random Spline is produced by passing Gaussian noise through a deep network that outputs spline parameters. This construction combines a structured function representation with a deep generative model and makes shape constraints easier to enforce. The authors use these random functions to model the intensity of each point process in neural population recordings.

Inference uses a variational autoencoder with a new recurrent encoder that accepts multiple point processes. The resulting model extracts a low-dimensional representation of population spiking activity. On a newly collected dataset from a primate performing a pedaling task, it provides better dimensionality reduction than the alternatives evaluated. The result supports the proposed representation for this neural-data application.
neurips-2019-deep-random-splines-for-poi.tldr: Deep Random Splines combine neural generators and constrained spline functions to model spike rates and improve neural population dimensionality reduction.

paragraphs: A signature transform represents a data stream through an infinite, graded collection of statistics. This collection characterizes the stream up to a negligible equivalence class. Earlier uses treated the transform as fixed preprocessing: compute signature features first, then train a separate model to use them.

This paper makes the transformation part of a learned architecture. A network learns an augmentation of the stream before the signature is computed, allowing signature terms to be selected in a way that depends on the data. The feature construction can therefore adapt during learning instead of being completely specified before the model is trained.

The authors also describe how to place a signature transform at other positions within a neural network, where it can be understood as a pooling operation. This broadens its role from an input representation to an internal component of deep models. The paper provides theoretical justification and supporting empirical experiments. Its main contribution is the integration of a mathematically grounded stream representation with learnable neural processing.
neurips-2019-deep-signature-transforms-6.tldr: The paper turns signature transforms from fixed stream features into adaptable components that can appear throughout a neural network.

paragraphs: Training with lower numerical precision offers a way to reduce computation time and energy use. Its theoretical analysis asks how rounding and limited numerical representation affect convergence. Earlier bounds for methods such as low-precision stochastic gradient descent often tied the required number of bits to the model's dimension.

That dependence means that, according to those bounds, maintaining a particular error guarantee requires more bits as the number of parameters grows. This paper derives new convergence bounds that omit the dimension term. The contribution is a sharper account of how low-precision training behaves as models scale, without an explicit penalty based on parameter count in these bounds.

The analysis also extends to other ways of representing numbers, including low-precision floating-point computation and logarithmic quantization. This makes the theoretical approach useful across multiple quantization schemes rather than only a single numerical format. The stated advance concerns convergence guarantees and their dependence on precision; the motivation is to better understand when reduced-precision computation can support scalable training.
neurips-2019-dimension-free-bounds-for-l.tldr: New convergence bounds remove explicit model-dimension dependence from analyses of low-precision training and extend to several quantization schemes.

paragraphs: Branch-and-bound solves combinatorial optimization problems by repeatedly dividing them into smaller search problems. Choosing which variable to branch on influences how that search proceeds. This paper learns that choice for mixed-integer linear programs, placing a neural decision policy inside the established optimization framework.

The model uses a graph with two kinds of nodes: variables and constraints. Their connections expose the problem's natural structure to a graph convolutional neural network. Training follows imitation learning, with the strong branching rule providing expert decisions. The network thus learns branching choices from an existing expert while using the relationships between variables and constraints as its representation.

Across a series of hard problems, the learned policies outperform previous machine-learning approaches to branching and transfer to instances substantially larger than those used for training. On large problems, the authors also report the first improvement over expert-designed branching rules in a state-of-the-art solver. These findings show that learned variable selection can improve an exact solver's search while generalizing beyond training-instance sizes.
neurips-2019-exact-combinatorial-optimiz.tldr: A graph neural network trained to imitate strong branching improves variable selection in an exact optimization solver and generalizes to larger instances.

paragraphs: The paper studies minimizing a sum of submodular set functions when a minimization routine is available for each individual component. These routines are called oracles: the overall algorithm can ask them to solve component problems. The computational question is how to combine their capabilities without making an excessive number of calls.

Existing approaches commonly convert the set problem into convex optimization using Lovász extensions and a squared Euclidean norm. This leads to a need for total variation oracles, which perform a more complex operation than ordinary component minimization. Without additional assumptions, implementing those operations may require many calls to the simpler oracles available in practice.

The authors modify the convex formulation so that it instead requires constrained total variation oracles. These can be solved using significantly fewer calls to the basic minimization routines. Results on graph cuts in two-dimensional and three-dimensional graphs support the claimed advantage. The central contribution is a reformulation that better matches the capabilities of the component solvers, reducing the work needed to use them.
neurips-2019-fast-decomposable-submodula.tldr: A modified convex formulation reduces the component-oracle calls needed to minimize sums of submodular functions.

paragraphs: Sparse Group Lasso fits a linear regression model while selecting both groups of features and individual features within groups. A standard solver uses block coordinate descent, updating one parameter group at a time. Although each update targets one group, computing it can depend on all groups or data points, making large problems expensive.

The proposed solver reduces this work by identifying groups whose parameters must be zero and skipping their updates. It makes these decisions using parameters from one group. It also gives priority to a candidate set containing groups whose parameters must be nonzero, concentrating updates on groups that matter to the fitted model.

The authors theoretically guarantee that their method produces the same results as the original block coordinate descent algorithm. Experiments show improved efficiency without reduced accuracy. This matters because the acceleration preserves the regression result: it changes how computational effort is allocated during optimization while retaining the solution behavior of the original method.
neurips-2019-fast-sparse-group-lasso-d37.tldr: The proposed Sparse Group Lasso solver skips provably zero groups and prioritizes useful updates while preserving the original solver's results.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning tries to make new tasks easier by learning from earlier ones. However, training the meta-learner can itself require large amounts of experience collected under its current policy. This paper targets that training burden, which can undermine the practical benefit of faster adaptation.

The approach distributes the work across individual off-policy learners that solve separate training tasks. A central meta-learner then imitates their solutions, consolidating them into a learned reinforcement learning procedure. Because the central learner learns from solutions, it can also accept demonstrations for some or all tasks. The same framework therefore accommodates both ordinary meta-RL and a mixture of learned task policies and examples.

In the ordinary setting, this enables reuse of previously learned policies without significant on-policy data collection during meta-training. Demonstrations offer another route when people can provide examples easily. Across continuous-control problems, the authors report substantial improvements in meta-RL sample efficiency over prior work and show that the approach can scale to tasks with visual observations.
neurips-2019-guided-meta-policy-search-7.tldr: Guided meta-policy search improves sample efficiency by training a central meta-learner to imitate separately learned task policies or demonstrations.

paragraphs: Generating an image from text requires translating a description into appearance, shape, and spatial arrangement. LeicaGAN organizes this task into three phases inspired by learning visual knowledge, imagining an overall picture, and progressively drawing its details. The phases form a single text-to-image generation framework.

First, a text-image encoder learns priors about semantics, texture, and color, while a text-mask encoder learns priors about shape and layout. Next, the model combines these complementary sources of information into an overall representation. Noise is added at this aggregation stage to support diverse generated images. This separates the acquisition of different kinds of visual knowledge from their combination for a particular description.

A cascaded attentive generator then creates an image from coarse structure toward finer detail. Adversarial learning encourages both visual realism and consistency with the description. Experiments on two public benchmark datasets show that LeicaGAN outperforms the baseline method. The reported findings support coordinating multiple learned priors with progressive generation to address the gap between textual meaning and visual content.
neurips-2019-learn-imagine-and-create-te.tldr: LeicaGAN combines learned appearance and layout priors with progressive image generation to improve text-to-image results over its evaluated baseline.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to reconstruct a probabilistic deterministic finite automaton from a black-box language model, such as a recurrent neural network. The aim is to obtain an automaton that represents the model's language behavior through states, transitions, and probabilities. This turns access to a trained model into a source of observations for learning another representation.

The algorithm adapts the L* exact-learning approach to probabilistic observations under noise. Two changes are central: it observes conditional probabilities, and it allows a tolerance when comparing observations. The tolerance lets the procedure accommodate variation rather than requiring all compared probabilistic observations to match exactly.

Applied to recurrent networks, the extracted automata achieve better or equal word error rate and normalized distributed cumulative gain compared with n-gram and weighted finite automata approximations of the same networks. The resulting models also represent a richer language class than n-grams and are guaranteed to be stochastic and deterministic, properties not guaranteed for the compared weighted automata.
neurips-2019-learning-deterministic-weig.tldr: A noise-tolerant adaptation of L* extracts probabilistic deterministic automata that match or outperform evaluated approximations of recurrent language models.

paragraphs: Person re-identification retrieves images of a particular person using a query image. The difficulty is that different people can share visible attributes, while the same person's appearance changes with viewpoint, pose, or scale. A useful representation must distinguish identities while handling these changes in appearance.

The paper proposes splitting image features into identity-related and identity-unrelated components. The first contains information useful for identifying a person, such as clothing; the second captures other variation, such as pose and scale. Its identity shuffle GAN, or IS-GAN, learns this factorization using identity labels without requiring auxiliary annotations for particular variation factors.

An identity-shuffling technique regularizes the separated features during learning. The goal is to learn a representation that handles multiple sources of appearance variation without supplying a separate supervisory signal for each one. Experiments show substantial improvements over the state of the art on Market-1501, CUHK03, and DukeMTMC-reID. These findings support the usefulness of separating identity information from other image factors for the evaluated retrieval tasks.
neurips-2019-learning-disentangled-repre.tldr: IS-GAN improves person re-identification by separating identity features from appearance variation using identity labels and an identity-shuffling regularizer.

paragraphs: This paper represents a three-dimensional shape by deforming and combining learned elementary structures. The representation makes the building blocks themselves learnable. The authors argue that this decomposition provides an interpretable account of shapes while improving both shape generation and matching between shapes.

They develop two complementary approaches within a deep learning framework. One learns continuous surface deformations, while the other learns structures expressed through three-dimensional points. Both approaches can also extend to abstract structures in higher dimensions, which the authors report can improve results. The shared idea is to learn useful underlying structures and then adapt them to represent particular shapes.

Evaluation covers object reconstruction on ShapeNet and dense correspondence estimation between human scans. The results are described as interpretable and repeatable in qualitative comparisons. Quantitatively, the authors report a 16% improvement for object generation through surface deformation and a 6% improvement over state-of-the-art correspondence results on the FAUST inter challenge. These findings support the representation across two substantially different geometric tasks.
neurips-2019-learning-elementary-structu.tldr: Learning elementary structures that can be deformed and combined improves both 3D object generation and matching between human scans.

paragraphs: A tiered interview process gathers information through stages such as resume screening, phone interviews, and site visits. Later stages offer more information but cost more. The paper studies how to allocate these assessments across a large applicant pool when the final goal is to select a strong cohort.

Using hiring models and structured interviews, the authors formulate the task as combinatorial pure exploration in a stochastic multi-armed bandit setting. Applicants correspond to arms, and the objective is to choose a subset satisfying a combinatorial structure. The formulation makes information gathering part of the selection problem: assessment resources should help determine which cohort to choose.

The authors provide algorithms for both probably approximately correct and fixed-budget settings, with provable guarantees for selecting a near-optimal cohort. Simulations using real data from a large US computer science graduate program show better selection decisions or lower budget use than the status quo. The empirical evidence concerns these simulations, while the theoretical contribution formalizes the tradeoff between assessment cost and informative selection.
neurips-2019-making-the-cut-a-bandit-bas.tldr: Bandit-based algorithms allocate costly interview stages to select near-optimal cohorts, with guarantees and favorable results in simulations using real applicant data.

paragraphs: MEG and EEG recordings can be summarized by covariance matrices describing how sensor signals vary together. Riemannian methods use the geometry of these matrices for prediction. However, artifact suppression often reduces their rank, creating difficulties for some geometric approaches. This paper studies regression directly from such reduced-rank covariance matrices.

The authors compare two approaches that convert covariance matrices into vectors through tangent-space projection. Wasserstein geometry directly accommodates reduced rank but lacks affine invariance. The alternative finds a shared subspace where the matrices become full rank, allowing an affine-invariant geometric distance. This gives two ways to handle the same preprocessing consequence while retaining a geometric representation.

Both distances allow perfect out-of-sample prediction on the studied synthetic generative models. On real data, age-prediction findings suggest that the methods outperform several sensor-space estimators and approach a source-localization model requiring MRI and substantial processing. These results suggest a role for data-driven geometric methods in automated large-scale M/EEG analysis, without equating synthetic-model perfection with real-data performance.
neurips-2019-manifold-regression-to-pred.tldr: Two geometric regression approaches handle reduced-rank MEG/EEG covariances and show promising prediction performance without source localization.

paragraphs: Testing whether revealing author identities causes peer-review bias requires separating actual bias from statistical artifacts. This paper examines both the hypothesis test and experimental design used in an earlier controlled conference study. Its negative results concern the reliability of detecting bias, rather than establishing that bias is absent.

The authors show that the earlier test does not guarantee control of false alarms. When relevant variables are correlated, measurement error, model mismatch, or reviewer calibration can each contribute to a high probability of declaring bias when none exists. They also show that non-blind reviewer bidding or a popular assignment procedure may inflate false alarms through the experimental setup itself.

The paper then develops a general testing framework and a test with guaranteed false-alarm control and nontrivial power even under the first three conditions. The bidding and assignment problems remain more fundamental design issues, not necessarily defects a different statistical test can fix. The contribution clarifies which problems require better inference and which require changes to how the experiment is organized.
neurips-2019-on-testing-for-biases-in-pe.tldr: The paper identifies false-alarm risks in peer-review bias studies and proposes a test robust to several statistical problems while distinguishing experimental-design issues.

paragraphs: Distributed training can spend substantial resources communicating updates between workers. Qsparse-local-SGD combines several ways to reduce that burden: sending sparse updates, quantizing their numerical values, and performing computation locally. The aim is to reduce transmitted information while maintaining effective optimization.

Compression changes the gradients that are communicated. The algorithm therefore tracks the difference between the true and compressed gradients through error compensation. This incorporates the compression discrepancy into the method instead of simply discarding it. The authors provide both synchronous and asynchronous implementations, covering two ways of coordinating distributed computation.

The convergence analysis addresses smooth convex and nonconvex objectives. For many important classes of sparsifiers and quantizers, Qsparse-local-SGD achieves the same convergence rate as ordinary distributed stochastic gradient descent. In experiments training ResNet-50 on ImageNet, it substantially reduces the number of transmitted bits needed to reach target accuracy compared with the state of the art. The theoretical and empirical results jointly support combining compression with local computation under the analyzed settings.
neurips-2019-qsparse-local-sgd-distribut.tldr: Qsparse-local-SGD combines compression, local computation, and error compensation to reduce communication while retaining standard convergence rates for many compression choices.

paragraphs: Photographs taken through glass often combine the scene behind the glass with a reflected scene. This paper tries to separate those two layers using just two captures: one unpolarized and one polarized image. The pair provides physical information about image formation while keeping the capture setup relatively simple.

Using fewer images creates a tradeoff. Compared with polarization methods requiring three or more captures, the separation problem has more unresolved ambiguity. The authors first estimate the orientation of the partially reflecting surface, which makes the physical image-formation problem well-posed. This estimation supplies structure needed to use the limited observations.

A refinement network then learns to separate the transmission and reflection layers, trained with a gradient loss. The approach thus combines physical constraints with learned refinement, addressing the ambiguity before refining the reconstructed layers. Quantitative and qualitative experiments show favorable performance against existing polarization-based and single-image solutions. The reported results support using this two-image setup to simplify acquisition while still obtaining effective reflection separation.
neurips-2019-reflection-separation-using.tldr: Surface-orientation estimation and learned refinement separate reflections from transmitted scenes using one polarized and one unpolarized image.

paragraphs: The paper connects the training and testing of residual networks with optimal control of transport equations. It uses this mathematical viewpoint to design an ensemble intended to improve a robustly trained model on both ordinary images and adversarially modified images. The theory motivates concrete changes to the networks and their predictions.

First, each residual mapping has Gaussian noise with a specified variance added to its output. Second, multiple modified ResNets are trained jointly, and their outputs are averaged to produce the final prediction. Together, these operations approximate the Feynman-Kac representation of a convection-diffusion equation's solution, linking noisy network computation and averaging to the underlying mathematical formulation.

On CIFAR10, the method reaches 85.62% accuracy on clean images and 57.94% robust accuracy under a 20-iteration IFGSM attack. The authors report that this exceeds the existing state of the art for defending against IFGSM on that benchmark. The evidence therefore supports improved clean and attack-specific performance for the evaluated ensemble.
neurips-2019-resnets-ensemble-via-the-fe.tldr: A mathematically motivated ensemble of noisy ResNets improves clean-image and IFGSM-attack accuracy on CIFAR10.

paragraphs: Synthetic humans provide richly labeled training data for 3D pose estimation, where obtaining real-world 3D labels is difficult. Yet models trained on synthetic color images often transfer poorly to real images. This paper investigates whether representing motion can help bridge that gap between simulated training data and real observations.

The authors preprocess the data to extract optical flow and the movement of two-dimensional keypoints. Standard neural-network approaches that perform poorly when trained on synthetic RGB images can perform well with these motion cues. The finding suggests that changing the information presented to the network can make synthetic training more useful when video is available.

Evaluation on the 3D Poses in the Wild dataset shows full 3D mesh recovery comparable to state-of-the-art methods trained on real 3D sequences. The proposed approach trains only on synthetic humans from SURREAL. These results support motion as a simple transfer strategy for the evaluated setting, with the availability of video being a stated condition for using the relevant cues.
neurips-2019-sim2real-transfer-learning-.tldr: Motion cues help models trained only on synthetic humans recover real-world 3D meshes at performance comparable to evaluated methods trained on real sequences.
